AL.text: Numbers on Alabama plates encode the county: 1 is Jefferson, 2 Mobile, 3 Montgomery, ranked by 1941 population.
Alabama license plates are made by inmates at Holman Correctional Facility's tag plant near Atmore.
Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery in 1955 for keeping her bus seat; the segregation law fell within a year.
Birmingham grew where iron ore, coal, and limestone occur together, a combination found nowhere else on Earth.
Alabama plates read Stars Fell On Alabama from 2002 to 2008, honoring an 1833 meteor storm that lit up the night sky.
Mobile's Cowbellion de Rakin Society paraded in 1830, decades before New Orleans held its first Mardi Gras parade.

AK.text: Wartime metal rationing put Alaska drivers on fiberboard plates from 1945 to 1948.
Cars and trains share one lane inside the 2.5-mile Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel to Whittier.
No road reaches Juneau, so the state capital is served only by ferry and plane.
Every Alaska resident who lives there over half the year gets an annual oil-wealth dividend check.
Utqiagvik, Alaska's northernmost town, sees no sunrise for about 65 days each winter.
Alaska's Big Dipper flag was designed by Benny Benson, a 13-year-old orphan, in a 1927 contest.

AZ.text: To boost its mining industry, Arizona stamped license plates from copper between 1932 and 1934.
London Bridge was shipped from England and rededicated at Lake Havasu City in October 1971.
Clocks in most of Arizona have skipped daylight saving time since 1968; the Navajo Nation observes it.
Removing a saguaro cactus from Arizona soil without a state permit can be a felony.
Two cavers kept Kartchner Caverns a secret from Arizona officials for 14 years to protect it.
Meteor Crater in Arizona trained Apollo astronauts to recognize the Moon's cratered ground.

AR.text: At Crater of Diamonds State Park near Murfreesboro, visitors keep any diamond they dig up.
Rain that fell in Arkansas about 4,000 years ago is only now surfacing as Hot Springs' hot water.
Some Arkansas land now sits east of the Mississippi River, stranded there when it shifted course.
US Army paratroopers escorted nine Black students into Little Rock's Central High School in 1957.
Al Capone kept a suite at Hot Springs' Arlington Hotel during decades of open illegal gambling there.
Arkansas Correctional Industries, staffed by state prison inmates, makes the state's license plates.

CA.text: Inmates at Folsom State Prison have been making California license plates since 1947.
A hacker took the vanity plate NULL hoping to vanish from ticket databases. He got $12,000 of other people's.
Until 1914 California issued no plates at all. Drivers made their own and bolted them on.
A San Luis Obispo lodging house coined the word motel when it opened in December 1925.
California brought back its black 1963-1969 plate after 7,500 drivers prepaid $50 for it in 2015.
California ran out of plate combinations in 2026 and flipped the format to 000AAA0.

CO.text: A mountain range has been the standard Colorado plate design since 1960, with a few years off.
US 550 between Ouray and Silverton, the Million Dollar Highway, runs cliffside without guardrails.
Colorado license plates are made by inmates at the Territorial Correctional Facility in Canon City.
A piece of Denver airport's giant blue mustang statue broke loose in the sculptor's studio and killed him.
Cross the Continental Divide on I-70 and rain on one side heads to the Pacific, the other to the Atlantic.
The Great Sand Dunes hum and boom when dry sand avalanches down their steep slopes.

CT.text: Connecticut drivers registered cars from 1903 but supplied their own plates until the state issued them in 1905.
In 1901 Connecticut set the first state speed limit: 12 mph in cities, 15 mph on country roads.
Hartford's Pope Manufacturing showed off its Columbia electric carriage in May 1897.
Connecticut's Constitution State motto honors its 1639 Fundamental Orders, not the US Constitution.
Connecticut license plates were made of porcelain, like bathroom tile, from 1905 to 1916.
Connecticut governors hand out prized low-digit plates 1 to 10,000, and each signals political favor.

DE.text: Delaware tag numbers are inherited and resold like property. Number 6 changed hands for $675,000.
A two-digit Delaware plate runs $125,000 to $350,000. Five digits will cost you about $700.
Delaware has numbered plates straight up from 1 since 1910, so a low one is a century of family history.
Any Delaware plate issued since 1942 can still go on a car with a current sticker.
Only a rear plate has been required in Delaware since 1945.
Delaware plates aren't made by a prison. They're stamped by Waldale Manufacturing in Nova Scotia, Canada.

FL.text: County names have appeared along the bottom of Florida plates since 1978.
Land speed records were set on the hard sand at Ormond and Daytona Beach from 1903 into the 1930s.
Florida license plates are stamped out by inmates at Union Correctional Institution near Raiford.
In 1980 a freighter lost in a squall rammed the Sunshine Skyway Bridge, dropping a span and a bus into Tampa Bay.
At Spook Hill in Lake Wales a slope with no visible horizon fools cars in neutral into seeming to roll uphill.
Fenced underpasses on I-75 let Florida panthers cross beneath traffic instead of into it.

GA.text: Georgia's 1941 plate was the first reflective general issue in the country.
Since 1971 Georgia plates have carried the name of the county that issued them.
A traffic reporter called Atlanta's five-level I-85 and I-285 interchange Spaghetti Junction in 1986.
A 56-foot steel chicken tops a Marietta KFC, and pilots use it to line up landings at nearby airports.
A bomb destroyed the Georgia Guidestones granite monument in 2022, and its remaining pieces were hauled away.
A dam above Toccoa Falls broke in 1977, sending a flood through Toccoa Falls College and killing 39 people.

HI.text: A rainbow has been screened across the standard Hawaii plate since 1991.
The Hana Highway on Maui packs in 620 curves and 59 bridges, 46 of them one lane wide.
Roadside billboards were outlawed in Hawaii in 1927, decades before statehood.
Road builders on the Pali in 1898 found 800 skulls, warriors driven off the cliff in an 1795 battle.
Unlike most states, Hawaii plates are not made by prisoners; a Portland, Oregon printer makes them.
Chain of Craters Road has been buried by lava so many times its far end now just stops at a hardened flow.

ID.text: The 1928 Idaho plate carried a large potato, one of the earliest pictures on an American plate.
Famous Potatoes has run along the bottom of Idaho plates since 1957.
The Perrine Bridge at Twin Falls is the one US structure open to BASE jumpers year round.
Evel Knievel's steam rocket failed to clear the Snake River Canyon on September 8, 1974.
Apollo astronauts studied volcanic rock at Craters of the Moon in Idaho in 1969.
Idaho inmates at Idaho Correctional Industries print, cut, and package the state's license plates.

IL.text: Wartime steel shortages had Illinois issuing soybean fiberboard plates from 1943 to 1948.
The first organized US auto race crossed Chicago snow on November 28, 1895, at about 7 mph.
The 1927 Illinois plate was the first to be embossed with the shape of the state.
Stateville prison made every Illinois plate in 1934, until the state's top court banned it in 1937.
Illinois punched holes in its 1912 front plates so they would not block the car's radiator airflow.
A ten-year-old's design, chosen from 400,000 student entries, became Illinois' 1976 bicentennial plate.

IN.text: Drivers here supplied their own plates until the state began issuing them on July 1, 1913.
Indianapolis Motor Speedway was paved with over three million bricks in 1909, hence the Brickyard.
Auburn keeps a museum of Auburn, Cord and Duesenberg cars in the old factory's office building.
Inmates paid about a dollar an hour made Indiana's plates until a private firm took over in 2015.
Indiana's covered-bridge plate honors Parke County, home to 31 of the roughly 1,000 left in the US.
Some 35 state capitols, the Empire State Building, and the Pentagon are built of Bedford, Indiana limestone.

IA.text: From 1922 to 1978 a number on the plate told you which of the 99 counties issued it.
Inmates at Anamosa State Penitentiary have made Iowa's license plates since 1926, over a million a year.
Riverside, Iowa declared itself Captain Kirk's future birthplace in 1985, and Gene Roddenberry approved.
Western Iowa's Loess Hills are wind-blown Ice Age silt; only one other place on Earth piles up this way, in China.
Iowa is the only U.S. state whose entire east and west borders are formed by rivers, the Mississippi and Missouri.
Iowa teens still hand-detassel rows of corn each July so seed companies can force cross-pollination for hybrid corn.

KS.text: Since 1951 a two-letter code on the plate has marked the county of registration.
Since 1975 Kansas plates have been made not by inmates but by Wichita workers with disabilities, at Center Industries.
Cheyenne Bottoms marsh in Kansas hosts up to 45% of all North American shorebirds each spring migration.
Monument Rocks chalk towers formed from a Kansas sea 80 million years ago, packed with fossils.
The original film reels of The Wizard of Oz are kept 650 feet underground in a Hutchinson, Kansas salt mine.
Kansas pioneers planted cottonwoods first because a thriving grove on treeless prairie meant there was water nearby.

KY.text: Chevrolet has built every Corvette in Bowling Green since 1981.
A sinkhole opened under the National Corvette Museum in 2014 and swallowed eight cars.
Kentucky's 1927 plate was the first in the US to name the issuing county; now it's a sticker at the bottom.
In 1935 Kentucky's governor made cafe owner Harland Sanders an honorary Colonel, 17 years before he founded KFC.
By law bourbon barrels can be used only once, so most get sold on to age Scotch whisky or Tabasco sauce.
About 95% of the world's bourbon is distilled in Kentucky.

LA.text: Louisiana is divided into parishes, so the roadside signs read parish line, not county line.
Inmates at Louisiana's Angola prison run the Tag Plant that stamps out the state's license plates.
A collapsed salt-mine cavern opened a Louisiana sinkhole in 2012 that swallowed trees and forced a town to evacuate.
A floodgate near Angola secretly keeps the Mississippi in its channel, away from the Atchafalaya.
Louisiana's civil law still traces to the Napoleonic Code, the only state not built on English common law.
Avery Island, home of Tabasco sauce, isn't surrounded by water; it's a 163-foot salt dome pushed up through the marsh.

ME.text: A red lobster sat behind the numbers from 1987 until a chickadee replaced it in 1999.
US Route 1 ends at Fort Kent, roughly 2,400 miles north of its start in Key West.
Maine license plates are stamped by inmates at Bolduc Correctional Facility in Warren.
Maine's 2026 plates, all 2 million of them, are stamped in Nova Scotia; the prison couldn't finish in time.
Maine is the only U.S. state that shares a border with just one other state, New Hampshire.
Maine's moose-hunt lottery draws about 70,000 entries a year for roughly 4,000 permits.

MD.text: Plates in 1934 carried the word Tercentenary for the colony's 300th anniversary.
Maryland's official state sport, since 1962, is jousting: spearing a small ring with a lance at a gallop.
At Hancock, Maryland narrows to just 1.8 miles between the Pennsylvania and West Virginia borders.
Maryland license plates are stamped by inmates at the Jessup Correctional Institution.
Fear of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge is so common a private service will drive your car across it for you.
Francis Scott Key wrote the national anthem from a truce ship while the British bombarded Fort McHenry in 1814.

MA.text: Plate number 1 went to Frederick Tudor, and his descendants still register it.
Massachusetts license plates are stamped by prisoners, now working out of MCI-Norfolk.
At the BU Bridge, a road crosses diagonally over a separate railroad bridge, both spanning the Charles River.
Cranberries float, so Massachusetts growers flood their bogs and comb the berries loose to harvest them.
Boston buried its elevated highway underground in the Big Dig, then planted a park, the Greenway, on top.
Fenway's Green Monster is 37 feet tall because the ballpark's left field was squeezed short by city streets.

MI.text: Plates read Water Wonderland through the 1950s, then Great Lake State from 1968.
Michigan license plates are made by inmates at Gus Harrison prison in Adrian, paid up to $1.31 an hour.
The Mackinac Bridge is repainted in a 7-year cycle that finishes only to start over again.
On Michigan Left intersections you cannot turn left; you go straight, then loop back at a median.
Michigan sued a driver over his WAR SUX plate; a federal court struck the ban down in 2014.
Michiganders south of the Mackinac Bridge get called trolls by Yoopers, for living under the bridge.

MN.text: 10,000 Lakes has been printed on Minnesota plates since 1950.
Plates whose serial begins with W are ordered by courts after certain drunk-driving cases.
Bob Dylan named a 1965 album for Highway 61, the road that runs past his birthplace, Duluth.
Minnesota license plates are stamped by inmates at the Rush City prison as part of MINNCOR Industries.
Minnesota plates get replaced every 7 years because their reflective coating fades and dims in headlights.
At Itasca State Park you can wade across the Mississippi River where it begins, just 18 inches deep.

MS.text: The issuing county's name has been stamped on Mississippi plates since the early 1940s.
US Highway 61 through the Delta is known as the Blues Highway.
Elvis Presley was born in a two-room house in Tupelo in 1935, and the house still stands.
During the 1863 siege, Vicksburg residents dug over 500 caves into hillsides to shelter from shelling.
Square ponds across the Mississippi Delta are catfish farms; the state grows half the nation's farmed catfish.
The US government once paid Mississippi farmers to plant kudzu for erosion control; it now blankets roadsides.

MO.text: Show-Me State has been on Missouri plates since 1979.
The Chain of Rocks Bridge over the Mississippi has a 22-degree bend in the middle.
Missouri license plates are made by inmates at the Jefferson City Correctional Center.
Missouri plates skip the letters I, O, and Q since they can be mistaken for 1 and 0 at a glance.
Painted barn roofs once advertised Meramec Caverns in 40 states; fewer than 50 survive today.
Missouri issued fiberboard license plates during WWII when metal was needed for the war effort.

MT.text: Numbers 1 to 56 on Montana plates stand for counties, ranked by their 1930 populations.
Plates carried Big Sky Country from 1967, shortened to Big Sky in 1976.
Front plates in 1913 and 1914 were perforated so air could reach the radiator.
Montana had no numbered daytime speed limit on its highways until 1999.
Montana license plates are made by inmates at Montana State Prison in Deer Lodge.
Near Butte, boulders at Ringing Rocks chime like bells when struck, but not once removed from the pile.

NE.text: Nebraska plates have carried a county number since 1922, ranked by how many cars each county had.
Carhenge, north of Alliance, copies Stonehenge using dozens of gray-painted American cars.
The Archway museum near Kearney was rolled across Interstate 80 in one piece one night in 1999.
Nebraskans incarcerated at the Nebraska State Penitentiary manufacture the state license plates.
Nebraska drivers once made their own plates from leather with metal numbers before the state issued any in 1915.
Only one plate per car was required in Nebraska from 1903 to 1920; a second plate became mandatory in 1921.

NV.text: Inmates made Nevada's plates at the Nevada State Prison from 1928 until the work moved in 2012.
Life magazine tagged Nevada's stretch of US 50 the Loneliest Road in America back in 1986.
A Reno man's real Nevada plate reading AREA 51 has drawn hundreds of erroneous toll tickets.
1950s Las Vegas hotels sold cocktails and rooftop seats so tourists could watch mushroom clouds from nuclear tests.
Nevada's Extraterrestrial Highway sign is stolen so often it now sits atop 20-foot poles.
Hoover Dam's concrete would have taken 75 years to cool alone, so engineers cooled it with 582 miles of ice-water pipe.

NH.text: New Hampshire inmates have stamped the state's plates since 1932, including the ones reading Live Free or Die.
A man who taped over Live Free or Die served 15 days in jail. In 1977 the Supreme Court said he never had to.
The rock profile on New Hampshire's plate collapsed in 2003. The state still pictures a face it no longer has.
Adults in cars here face no seat belt requirement, which is not the case anywhere else.
The Kancamagus Highway crosses about 34 miles of national forest with no gas station on the way.
New Hampshire's state prison makes about half a million license plates a year, nearly every one used in the state.

NJ.text: A 1949 law still keeps New Jersey drivers from pumping their own gasoline.
Jughandle ramps send New Jersey drivers to the right so they can then turn left across the road.
New Jersey inmates at Bayside State Prison make more than a million license plates every year.
Pulaski Skyway banned trucks in 1934, two years after opening, for being too narrow and steep. The ban still stands.
New Jersey's Conserve Wildlife plate helps fund bald eagles' comeback from one nest in the 1980s to over 220 today.
A 131-foot tower in Edison, NJ, topped with a giant light bulb, marks where Edison's bulb first glowed.

NM.text: New Mexico prints USA on its plates so nobody mistakes the state for the country to the south.
Twenty-seven radio dishes sit on rails beside US 60 west of Socorro so crews can reposition them.
From 1947 to 1972, New Mexico plates coded your county by size: Santa Fe County was always number 1.
Visiting the Trinity atomic bomb site means showing your car registration and insurance at the gate.
New Mexico only bolts a plate to the rear of the car, so the front bumper legally stays bare.
A 1974 steel shortage forced New Mexico to issue some plates made of paper instead of metal.

NY.text: New York became the first state to require car registration, in 1901, using the owner's initials.
Blue numbers on reflective orange marked New York plates from 1973 to 1986.
Prisoners at the Auburn Correctional Facility stamp out New York's license plates.
Some 2020 Excelsior plates were recalled because their shine defeated toll and speed cameras.
From 1973 to 1986, AUB-prefix plates marked Cayuga County, home to the Auburn prison plate factory.
New York planned to force out plates older than ten years in 2020, but driver backlash killed the rule.

NC.text: Orville Wright flew 120 feet in 12 seconds over Kill Devil Hills on December 17, 1903.
A First in Freedom slogan arrived in 1975 and was dropped within a few years after objections.
North Carolina plate serials went blue to red in 2007, then back after drivers found red hard to read.
From 1926 to 1931, North Carolina plate serials sorted cars into horsepower classes A through E.
Dare County residents can request OBX-lettered plates naming the Outer Banks on any state design.
Since 2015 North Carolina drivers pick from three plate slogans: First in Flight, First in Freedom, or In God We Trust.

ND.text: Peace Garden State has ridden along on North Dakota plates since 1956.
Geese in Flight, a 110-foot scrap metal sculpture, stands where the Enchanted Highway meets I-94.
Salem Sue, a 38-foot fiberglass Holstein, has watched Interstate 94 from New Salem since 1974.
North Dakota's license plates are made by inmates at the state penitentiary's Rough Rider Industries.
Rugby, ND claimed North America's geographic center for 90 years, until a 2017 recalculation moved it to Center, ND.
Ten twisted steel girders from the World Trade Center form a 9/11 memorial in North Dakota's Peace Garden.

OH.text: About 35,000 Ohio plates from 2021 were shredded because the Wright Flyer flew backwards.
Birthplace of Aviation has appeared on Ohio plates since 1997.
Zanesville's Y-shaped bridge splits in midair where the Licking River joins the Muskingum.
Ohio's license plates are made by inmates at Lebanon Correctional via Ohio Penal Industries.
Newark, Ohio has a 7-story office shaped like a picnic basket, its steel handles heated so they won't ice up.
Cleveland's Cuyahoga River caught fire so often the 1969 blaze helped spur the Clean Water Act.

OK.text: The world's first parking meter went up in Oklahoma City on July 16, 1935, at a nickel an hour.
Tulsa's Cyrus Avery pressed for the number 66 on the Chicago-to-Los Angeles highway in 1926.
A concrete blue whale built beside Route 66 near Catoosa began as a 1972 anniversary gift.
An Osage battle shield sat at the center of Oklahoma plates issued starting in 1989.
A 66-foot steel soda bottle has lit up Route 66 at Arcadia since 2007.
Oklahoma plate codes are two letters from the county name, except OK for Oklahoma County and TU for Tulsa.

OR.text: Drivers could not pump their own fuel in Oregon until a law changed that in 2023.
A Douglas fir has stood in the middle of standard Oregon plates since 1988.
Buying an Oregon salmon plate has sent extra money to watershed work since 1998.
Portland's name was decided by a coin flip in 1845; the winning penny is kept at the Oregon Historical Society.
At the Oregon Vortex, two people who swap places appear to shrink or grow, a floor-tilt illusion near Gold Hill.
Every Oregon beach is public land under a 1967 law, so you can walk all 363 miles of coast for free.

PA.text: Turnpike crews reused railroad tunnels that had sat unfinished in the mountains since the 1880s.
You've Got a Friend in Pennsylvania rode on plates from 1983 to 1987.
Pennsylvania cars have needed only a rear plate since 1952.
Pennsylvania inmates at SCI Fayette manufacture the state's license plates as prison labor.
The abandoned Sideling Hill Turnpike tunnel, closed since 1968, is now open to hikers and cyclists.
Some Pennsylvania Amish have been fined or jailed for refusing the orange slow-vehicle triangle on buggies.

RI.text: Low-numbered Rhode Island plates have been handed out as political favors for over a century.
A 58-foot fiberglass termite has loomed over Interstate 95 in Providence since 1980.
A Newport judge handed down a jail sentence for speeding in 1904.
Rhode Island inmates at the ACI make the state's license plates as part of a prison job program.
Rhode Island is one of the few states letting you will your license plate to a family member.
The Fox Point Hurricane Barrier can lower three river gates to seal Providence off from a storm surge.

SC.text: From 1930 to 1933 the plates advertised the state as The Iodine State.
South of the Border opened near Dillon in 1949 and now advertises along I-95 for hundreds of miles.
Inmates at Broad River Correctional Institution in Columbia stamp about 800,000 South Carolina license plates a year.
South Carolina cars need only a rear plate; state law never required a front one.
Gaffney's water tower along I-85 is painted as a giant peach, complete with a cleft and a leaf.
Only 3 of 170 North American firefly species sync their flashes, and Congaree is one of the few places to see it.

SD.text: The first digit on a South Dakota plate is a county code, and Minnehaha County holds number 1.
Wall Drug began advertising free ice water in 1936, and travelers still pull off the highway for it.
The Corn Palace in Mitchell gets new murals made from ears of corn nearly every year.
South Dakota's license plates are stamped by inmates at the State Penitentiary in Sioux Falls.
A vault called the Hall of Records, carved behind Lincoln's head at Rushmore, was never finished.
Wind Cave breathes: air rushes through its narrow entrance as outside barometric pressure shifts.

TN.text: From 1936 to 1956 Tennessee cut its license plates into the outline of the state.
US 129 at Deals Gap packs 318 curves into 11 miles and is nicknamed the Tail of the Dragon.
Great Smoky Mountains National Park charges no entrance fee because of a deed condition on Newfound Gap Road.
Tennessee's license plates for all 95 counties are made by inmates at a TRICOR prison plant in Nashville.
Bristol Motor Speedway's track is concrete, which grips better than asphalt because heat doesn't soften it.
Jack Daniel's is distilled in Lynchburg, Tennessee, a dry county where buying a drink is still illegal.

TX.text: Ten Cadillacs were buried nose-down in an Amarillo field in 1974 to create Cadillac Ranch.
A sign at Adrian marks the Route 66 midpoint, 1,139 miles from both Chicago and Los Angeles.
Houston's Katy Freeway reaches 26 lanes across when frontage roads and toll lanes are counted.
Texas license plates are stamped by inmates at the Wynne prison unit in Huntsville, nearly 11 million a year.
Texas's 1845 annexation deal lets it split into five states someday, but says nothing about seceding.
Any state's flag may fly as high as the US flag; the idea that only Texas may is a myth.

UT.text: Utah's 1944 plates were pressed from soybean-based fiberboard because metal was needed for the war.
Delicate Arch has appeared on Utah passenger plates since 1992.
Skiers and the phrase Greatest Snow on Earth have been on Utah plates since 1985.
Malcolm Campbell drove 301 mph across the Bonneville Salt Flats in September 1935.
Interstate 70 crosses the San Rafael Swell with no gas, food, or lodging for over 100 miles.
Utah is switching new plates from embossed (raised) numbers to flat-screen printing starting in 2025.

VT.text: Vermont banned billboards in 1968, and the last one came down in 1974.
Vermont plates from 1905 to 1909 were made of porcelain rather than plain metal.
Route 108 through Smugglers Notch is too tight for tractor-trailers and closes each winter.
Vermont's 1942-43 plates got yellow metal tabs instead of new plates, to save metal for the war.
Congress briefly declared Lake Champlain the sixth Great Lake in 1998, reversing it 18 days later.
Montpelier is the only U.S. state capital with no McDonald's or Starbucks.

VA.text: Virginia's first plates, issued in 1906, were white lettering baked onto black porcelain.
Virginia is for Lovers started as a 1969 tourism ad and reached the standard plate in 2014.
Skyline Drive runs 105 miles through Shenandoah National Park with a 35 mph limit and 75 overlooks.
The Blue Ridge Parkway begins at Rockfish Gap where Skyline Drive ends, then runs 469 miles south.
One in ten personalized license plates in the entire U.S. is registered in Virginia.
A 2022 DNA study tied Chincoteague's wild ponies to a 500-year-old Spanish horse tooth from Puerto Rico.

WA.text: Washington license plates have been made by incarcerated workers since 1923.
The first Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted apart in a windstorm on November 7, 1940.
Washington plates have used a letter prefix since 1935 to encode which county issued them.
Four Franciscan nuns ran the Shaw Island ferry terminal, working its ramps, from 1976 to 2004.
Washington State Ferries are numbered state routes, like SR 304 and SR 305, not just boats.
Washington leaves out letters I, O, and Q on plates so they are not mistaken for 1 and 0.

WV.text: West Virginia has required only a rear license plate since 1944.
One Saturday each October the New River Gorge Bridge closes to traffic for Bridge Day.
Cell phones and Wi-Fi are banned near Green Bank, WV, so a giant radio telescope can hear the sky.
Inmates at West Virginia's Mount Olive prison made over 469,000 license plates in 2020 alone.
Months after locals reported a winged 'Mothman,' Point Pleasant's Silver Bridge collapsed, killing 46.
Neither writer of Country Roads had set foot in West Virginia; the drive that inspired it was in Maryland.

WI.text: In May 1918 Wisconsin became the first place anywhere to post numbered route signs on its highways.
Harley-Davidson's first motorcycles were built in a 10-by-15-foot Milwaukee shed in 1903.
Surplus World War II amphibious trucks have carried sightseers around Wisconsin Dells since 1946.
Since May 2024 Wisconsin plates on EVs and hybrids get an orange EV HYBRID sticker for responders.
Wisconsin Dells was called Kilbourn City until 1931, when it renamed itself after the sandstone dells.
Fresh Wisconsin cheese curds squeak against your teeth, a squeak that fades within about 12 hours.

WY.text: The number on a Wyoming plate marks the county, ranked in the 1930s by assessed property value.
Wyoming's 1944 plates were made of soybean-based fiberboard to save metal for the war effort.
Yellowstone's Grand Loop Road is a 142-mile figure eight, and cars were first allowed in during 1915.
In 1941 a parachutist landed atop Devils Tower on a stunt and was stranded there for six days.
In the 1880s tourists tossed dirty laundry into Old Faithful and fished it out clean after it erupted.
Wyoming legislators tried to repeal women's right to vote in 1871; the governor's veto held by one vote.

DC.text: Taxation Without Representation was added to District plates in November 2000.
Presidents differ on the protest plates: George W. Bush removed them, Barack Obama restored them in 2013.
The street grid skips J Street because I and J looked alike in 18th-century handwriting.
Congress capped DC building heights at street width plus 20 feet after the 1894 Cairo Hotel alarmed neighbors.
DC's flag borrows its three stars and two bars from George Washington's own family coat of arms.
Wartime metal shortages left DC cars with only a rear plate from 1945 to 1946, revalidated by colored tabs.

PR.text: Isla del Encanto, meaning Island of Enchantment, is the slogan on Puerto Rican plates.
The plates carry a drawing of the old Spanish fort guarding San Juan harbor.
Road distances are posted in kilometers while speed limits are posted in miles per hour.
Gasoline on the island is priced and pumped by the liter instead of the gallon.
Puerto Rico has needed only a rear license plate since 1976, leaving the front bumper bare.
Since 2012 Puerto Rico drivers can pay extra for a narrow, European-sized plate instead of the standard one.

ON.text: Yours to Discover replaced Keep it Beautiful on Ontario license plates in 1982.
An Orange Order leader's 1948 protest forced Ontario to restore the crown symbol on its license plates.
Ontario license plate serials skip the letters G, I, O, Q and U so they cannot be confused with numbers.
Since 1983 an Ontario plate sticker expires in the registrant's birth month, spreading renewals year-round.
Kitchener, Ontario was called Berlin until a 1916 wartime vote, held under pressure from soldiers, renamed it.
Atikokan, Ontario keeps Eastern Standard Time year-round, skipping the switch to daylight saving entirely.

QC.text: The 1967 Quebec plates marked Expo 67 and the centennial, with different designs front and back.
In December 2008 Quebec became the first place in North America to require winter tires.
Quebec's Global Strategic Maple Syrup Reserve stockpiles enough syrup to steady world prices when a harvest fails.
Quebec's motto "Je me souviens" gives no object, so its exact meaning has been argued over for a century.
Quebec alone runs on a civil code descended from Napoleon's, while every other province uses British common law.
Fresh cheese curds squeak on your teeth for about a day, until lactic acid cuts up the stretchy proteins.

BC.text: The first plates British Columbia issued, in 1913, were porcelain baked onto iron.
Vancouver drivers moved from the left side of the road to the right on January 1, 1922.
Near Field, trains loop through two spiral tunnels cut into the mountains and opened in 1909.
From 1931 to 1975, British Columbia license plates were stamped out by inmates at Oakalla Prison.
British Columbia named the spirit bear its mammal emblem: a black bear turned white by one recessive gene, not albinism.
Fraser River sockeye salmon navigate the open ocean by magnetic field, then switch to scent to find their birth stream.

AB.text: Alberta stopped requiring a front plate in 1992.
Six wildlife overpasses and 38 underpasses help animals cross the Trans-Canada Highway in Banff.
Highway 3 through the Crowsnest Pass runs across limestone dumped by the 1903 Frank Slide.
A chinook wind once pushed Pincher Creek from -19C to 22C, a 41-degree jump, in a single hour.
Every Alberta plate is stamped in Amherst, Nova Scotia, over 4,000 km away, by Waldale Manufacturing.
The Rockies force moist prairie air skyward into a low freezing layer, fueling Calgary hailstorms.

MB.text: No road reaches Churchill, so travellers arrive by train or plane.
Walkers were barred from crossing Portage and Main in Winnipeg from 1979 until June 2025.
Bears that wander into Churchill are held in a cinderblock "jail," unfed, until Hudson Bay ice lets them go.
A grassy 30km ditch called Duff's Ditch quietly reroutes the Red River around Winnipeg during spring floods.
Manitoba Hydro sells surplus power to Minnesota, then buys back Minnesota wind power when its own demand peaks.
A sign east of Winnipeg marks Canada's longitudinal center, the line midway between its far east and far west points.

SK.text: Every Mountie trains at Depot Division in Regina, which has taught recruits since 1885.
Grid roads cross the farmland about a mile apart, laying a checkerboard over the province.
Moose Jaw gave its statue Mac the Moose bigger antlers in 2019 to outmeasure a rival in Norway.
Saskatchewan's potash sits over a kilometre down, salt left when a sea evaporated 390 million years ago.
Deep Bay on Reindeer Lake is a near-perfect circle 220m deep, carved by a meteorite about 99 million years ago.
Cypress Hills poked above the last ice sheet, letting species like a rare mountainsnail survive the ice age.

NS.text: Nova Scotia switched from driving on the left to driving on the right in 1923.
License plates for several Canadian provinces are manufactured in Amherst, Nova Scotia.
Nova Scotia still sends Boston a Christmas tree every year, thanking it for aid after the 1917 Halifax Explosion.
Sable Island's wild horses are legally protected; touching or feeding one without a permit is against Canadian law.
Rocks at Peggy's Cove that look wet and dark mark exactly where a sudden rogue wave has already reached.
Some Cape Breton town-limit signs give the name in Scottish Gaelic, a language still taught locally today.

NB.text: Since 2009 New Brunswick plates have carried a slogan in both English and French.
New Brunswick moved to right-hand driving at midnight on December 1, 1922.
Hartland's bridge was built open in 1901 and only got its roof after ice wrecked two spans in 1920.
At Hopewell Rocks the Fundy tide drops far enough for visitors to walk on the sea floor.
Twice daily the Bay of Fundy sends a wave up Moncton's Petitcodiac River, against its current.
In Moncton's Chiac dialect, Acadians bolt English verbs onto French endings, like washer for to wash.

NL.text: Newfoundland was a separate dominion when it issued its first license plates in 1925.
Drivers here kept to the left until 1947, two years before Newfoundland joined Canada.
Newfoundland and Labrador is the one province that does not offer personalized plates.
Moose warning signs line the highways; roughly 125,000 moose live on the island.
Clocks here run half an hour ahead of Atlantic time, an offset found nowhere else in North America.
Newfoundland's floral emblem, the pitcher plant, drowns insects in a pool of enzymes in its leaves.

PE.text: Prince Edward Island banned cars from its roads in 1908 and did not lift the ban fully until 1919.
After 1913 Islanders were allowed to drive only on three set days of the week.
Bridge tolls are collected only as you leave the Island, never on the way in.
Cyclists and walkers may not cross the Confederation Bridge, so a shuttle carries them over.
Anne of Green Gables appeared on Island plates from 1993 to 1997, then the new bridge took her place.
Prince Edward Island's red soil gets its color from iron oxide in the sandstone, plain rust.

NT.text: Northwest Territories plates have been cut in the shape of a polar bear since 1970.
The Inuvik to Tuktoyaktuk highway opened in November 2017, the first Canadian road to the Arctic Ocean.
The Tibbitt to Contwoyto winter road is built mostly on frozen lakes and lasts about two months.
Inuvik pipes its water and sewer lines above ground in insulated boxes, since permafrost there is too deep to bury them.
Before the Deh Cho Bridge, Mackenzie River crossings shut for weeks each spring between the ice road and the ferry.
Inuvik's Catholic church is built round like an igloo so frost heave rocks it gently instead of cracking it apart.

YT.text: A gold panner has been stamped on Yukon license plates since 1952.
Yukon's 1979 issue was the last plate in Canada made to last only a single year.
A homesick soldier nailed up a sign to his Illinois home town in 1942, starting the Sign Post Forest.
The Dempster Highway leaves the Klondike Highway near Dawson City and stays gravel for 737 kilometres.
A free ferry carries cars over the Yukon River at Dawson City to the Top of the World Highway.
From 1976 to 1981, a Yukon plate's first letter named your town: D was Dawson, F Faro, H Haines Junction.

NU.text: Nunavut kept the bear-shaped plate when it separated from the Northwest Territories in 1999.
A rectangular plate designed by an Iqaluit resident replaced the bear shape in 2012.
That rectangular design carried 25 stars, one for each community in the territory.
No road links Nunavut to the rest of Canada, so vehicles arrive by barge or cargo plane.
New Nunavut plates spell the territory in English and Inuktitut syllabics, split by a stone inuksuk.
Arctic buildings often stand on stilts sunk deep in the ground so summer heat can't melt the frozen soil beneath.
